cards.front: Before anyone had purified an adrenaline receptor, what experimental evidence led Raymond Ahlquist to separate adrenergic receptors into alpha and beta types?
cards.back: He ranked adrenaline-like compounds by their order of potency across tissues, revealing two distinct tissue-response patterns corresponding to alpha and beta receptors.
cards.quote: In 1948 Raymond Ahlquist sorted adrenaline-like compounds by their order of potency across tissues and defined two receptor types, alpha and beta.
cards.section: A decoy in the receptor: fit without the push

cards.front: In receptor pharmacology, {{c1::affinity}} measures how tightly a molecule fits a binding site, whereas efficacy measures how strongly it switches the receptor on.
cards.quote: That separated two properties from the lesson on binding and dose-response: affinity (how tightly a molecule fits the site) and efficacy (how strongly it switches the receptor on).
cards.section: A decoy in the receptor: fit without the push

cards.front: A drug with affinity for a receptor's hormone-binding site and without agonist efficacy is an {{c1::antagonist}}.
cards.quote: A molecule with affinity and without agonist efficacy is an antagonist—a key that enters a lock and will not turn, keeping adrenaline out
cards.section: A decoy in the receptor: fit without the push

cards.front: How does blocking beta-adrenergic receptors with propranolol relieve angina in a heart with narrowed arteries?
cards.back: It occupies the beta receptor without turning it on, blunting the heart's response to adrenaline so the heart demands less oxygen.
cards.quote: blunt the heart's response to adrenaline so it asks for less oxygen.
cards.section: A decoy in the receptor: fit without the push

cards.front: Besides beta-receptor antagonists like propranolol, what ulcer drug did James Black develop using the same decoy strategy, and which receptor does it block?
cards.back: Cimetidine, which blocks histamine receptors in the stomach lining.
cards.quote: Black later applied the same idea to histamine receptors in the stomach lining, yielding the ulcer drug cimetidine.
cards.section: A decoy in the receptor: fit without the push

cards.front: A compound binds beta-adrenergic receptors tightly, blocking adrenaline, yet shifts the receptor partway active on its own (like dichloroisoprenaline). In a resting heart with very little adrenaline, does it slow or speed the heart, and why?
cards.back: It speeds the heart. When endogenous adrenaline is scarce at rest, the compound's partial agonist efficacy stimulates receptors rather than merely blocking stronger adrenaline activation.
cards.why: In tissues or states with abundant adrenaline, the same tight-binding partial agonist can block full adrenaline stimulation, explaining why dichloroisoprenaline acted as a blocker in some tests and a stimulant in others.
cards.quote: Speeds it: partial efficacy stimulates receptors when adrenaline is scarce, as dichloroisoprenaline did in some tissues.
cards.section: A decoy in the receptor: fit without the push

cards.front: Around 1990, why did designing a selective small-molecule inhibitor for one protein kinase's ATP pocket look implausible?
cards.back: About 500 human protein kinases catalyse the same transfer of ATP's end phosphate onto a protein, so their active pockets fold into nearly the same shape.
cards.quote: ~500 human protein kinases catalyse the same transfer of ATP's end phosphate onto a protein, so their active pockets fold into nearly the same shape.
cards.section: One pocket, five hundred kinases: how imatinib became selective

cards.front: Chronic myeloid leukaemia is caused by {{c1::BCR-ABL}}, a fused, always-on tyrosine kinase absent from healthy blood cells.
cards.quote: Chronic myeloid leukaemia offered a clean test: one fused, always-on tyrosine kinase, BCR-ABL, causes it, and healthy blood cells do not normally have it.
cards.section: One pocket, five hundred kinases: how imatinib became selective

cards.front: What did Juerg Zimmermann's group show when they added a single methyl group to a phenylaminopyrimidine kinase-inhibitor core?
cards.back: That single methyl group removed activity against protein kinase C while preserving ABL inhibition, demonstrating that small chemical changes can tune kinase selectivity.
cards.quote: one added methyl group removed activity against protein kinase C while keeping ABL inhibition.
cards.section: One pocket, five hundred kinases: how imatinib became selective

cards.front: In Elisabeth Buchdunger's pharmacology panel, which three kinases did imatinib hit while barely touching the EGF and insulin receptors?
cards.back: ABL, the PDGF receptor, and KIT.
cards.quote: Elisabeth Buchdunger's pharmacology panel showed what the lead compound hit: ABL and the PDGF receptor, and later KIT, with the EGF and insulin receptors barely touched.
cards.section: One pocket, five hundred kinases: how imatinib became selective

cards.front: How does biochemical selectivity differ from cellular (therapeutic) selectivity for a kinase inhibitor like imatinib?
cards.back: Biochemical selectivity is the molecule's short target list on purified enzymes and in cells; cellular selectivity is the disease's lethal dependence on the target compared with normal cells.
cards.quote: Biochemical selectivity belongs to the molecule: its short target list on purified enzymes and in cells.
cards.section: One pocket, five hundred kinases: how imatinib became selective

cards.front: How is binding ABL's idle (switched-off) conformation thought to help imatinib achieve selectivity across about 500 kinases?
cards.back: Switched-off shapes are thought to diverge across kinases more than active working shapes do, though how much of imatinib's selectivity this explains is still studied.
cards.quote: switched-off shapes are thought to diverge across kinases more than working shapes do, though how much of the selectivity this explains is still studied.
cards.section: One pocket, five hundred kinases: how imatinib became selective

cards.front: Imatinib inhibits ABL, the PDGF receptor, and KIT—all used by normal cells—yet in culture it stops BCR-ABL leukaemia colonies while sparing normal colonies. What does this result demonstrate?
cards.back: Cellular (therapeutic) selectivity driven by target dependence: dividing leukaemia cells die without BCR-ABL, whereas normal cells can get through a period without ABL, the PDGF receptor, and KIT.
cards.why: Because this layer depends on how living cells respond to losing each kinase, it can only be measured in living cells or patients, not on purified enzymes.
cards.quote: Cellular (therapeutic) selectivity belongs to the disease: dividing leukaemia cells die without BCR-ABL, whereas normal cells get through a period without ABL, the PDGF receptor, and KIT.
cards.section: One pocket, five hundred kinases: how imatinib became selective

cards.front: Small-molecule drugs targeting a kinase's {{c1::ATP pocket}} include imatinib, gefitinib, erlotinib, and the JAK inhibitors.
cards.quote: That is the second class: a small molecule in a kinase's ATP pocket—imatinib (2001), gefitinib (2003), erlotinib (2004), and the JAK inhibitors from the JAK-STAT lesson.
cards.section: One pocket, five hundred kinases: how imatinib became selective

cards.front: Position 315 in ABL is the {{c1::gatekeeper residue}}, guarding a deeper alcove beside the ATP pocket.
cards.quote: Position 315 is ABL's gatekeeper residue, guarding a deeper alcove beside the ATP pocket.
cards.section: When the drug stops working: one residue changed

cards.front: How does the BCR-ABL T315I mutation defeat imatinib without stopping ATP-driven phosphorylation?
cards.back: Bulkier isoleucine breaks imatinib's hydrogen bond with threonine 315 and sterically blocks the deeper alcove, which ATP does not need for catalysis.
cards.why: Mutating the gatekeeper shifts ABL toward its active shape and can even raise its catalytic activity.
cards.quote: Bulkier isoleucine breaks that contact and sterically blocks imatinib, yet ATP does not need the alcove, so the kinase keeps working
cards.section: When the drug stops working: one residue changed

cards.front: When relapsed patients' BCR-ABL is sequenced, a point mutation appears at one drug-contact residue while leaving catalysis intact. What two conclusions does this observation support?
cards.back: It provides strong evidence that imatinib was working through BCR-ABL and that the relapsed tumour still depended on BCR-ABL to survive.
cards.quote: Selecting a change at one drug contact while leaving catalysis intact is strong evidence that imatinib worked through BCR-ABL and that the tumour still depended on it.
cards.section: When the drug stops working: one residue changed

cards.front: How do ponatinib and asciminib each overcome the BCR-ABL T315I gatekeeper mutation?
cards.back: Ponatinib passes bulky isoleucine 315 using a slim carbon-carbon triple bond, while asciminib bypasses the ATP pocket by binding a separate site on ABL.
cards.why: By contrast, second-generation dasatinib kills cells with mutations such as G250E, yet T315I resists dasatinib too.
cards.quote: Ponatinib passes isoleucine 315 with a slim carbon-carbon triple bond; asciminib bypasses the pocket by binding a separate site on ABL.
cards.section: When the drug stops working: one residue changed

cards.front: Relapsed leukaemia cells are treated with imatinib in culture: phosphorylation of a direct BCR-ABL substrate stays low, yet the cells keep dividing. Is resistance due to T315I, extra BCR-ABL copies, or a bypass, and why?
cards.back: A bypass outside BCR-ABL. Either T315I or extra BCR-ABL copies would restart BCR-ABL and restore direct-substrate phosphorylation; a persistently low signal means BCR-ABL remains blocked.
cards.quote: T315I or extra BCR-ABL copies restart BCR-ABL and restore direct-substrate phosphorylation; a low signal means BCR-ABL stays blocked.
cards.section: When the drug stops working: one residue changed

cards.front: Relapsed leukaemia cells exposed to the standard kinase-inhibitor dose show nearly full phosphorylation of a direct target substrate, no sequence change in the kinase domain, and fivefold extra copies of the kinase gene. What caused resistance, and what drug strategy fits?
cards.back: Gene amplification makes more unchanged kinase than that dose can cover. Because the pocket is unaltered, a higher dose or a tighter-binding inhibitor of the same pocket may work if safely tolerated.
cards.quote: The target is unchanged, so a higher dose or a tighter-binding inhibitor of the same pocket may work, if that much inhibition can be reached safely.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Sequencing a relapsed tumour's kinase gene reveals a point mutation in the kinase domain. What two experimental steps confirm that this mutation caused resistance to the inhibitor?
cards.back: Compare the relapse sequence against a pre-treatment sample to confirm the mutation arose at relapse, then test the purified mutant enzyme to show it needs far more drug for inhibition.
cards.quote: Sequence the kinase gene at relapse and compare it with the sample from before treatment, then show that the purified mutant enzyme needs far more drug.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A patient's leukaemia relapses after a year on a kinase inhibitor. Starting from one assay in drug-treated patient cells, design a diagnostic workflow that separates target mutation, target amplification, and pathway bypass, and pairs each with a second-drug strategy.
cards.back: By the direct-substrate rule, first measure phosphorylation of a direct target substrate with the drug present. If restored, sequence the kinase (mutation: avoid that contact or bind a separate site) and count gene copies and protein (amplification: higher dose or tighter pocket inhibitor). If low, measure downstream phosphorylation to identify the bypass kinase and add a drug against it or the shared downstream step alongside the first drug.
cards.quote: In the patient's cells, with the drug present, measure phosphorylation of a protein that the kinase phosphorylates directly.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A typical protein kinase sees cellular ATP at ~1 mM (Km ~10 µM). A reversible ATP-pocket drug reaches 2 µM inside cells with Kd = 5 nM. Using [ligand]/Kd ratios, calculate the drug's approximate fractional share of the pocket.
cards.quote: Side by side, the [ligand] / Kd ratio explains why cellular ATP is beatable while cellular GTP is not:
cards.section: The target nobody could hit: a bond to the mutation itself

cards.front: K-Ras binds GTP with Kd ~10 pM in a cell holding ~0.5 mM GTP. A reversible nucleotide-site drug reaches 2.5 µM inside cells with Kd = 1 nM. Using [ligand]/Kd ratios, calculate roughly what fraction of K-Ras holds the drug.
cards.quote: Side by side, the [ligand] / Kd ratio explains why cellular ATP is beatable while cellular GTP is not:
cards.section: The target nobody could hit: a bond to the mutation itself

cards.front: For K-Ras (cellular GTP ~0.5 mM, Kd ~10 pM), suppose a reversible nucleotide-site drug reaches 5 µM inside cells. Using the [ligand]/Kd occupancy rule, calculate what drug Kd would be needed for 50% occupancy of K-Ras and state what this implies.
cards.back: By the [ligand]/Kd competition rule, 50% occupancy requires [drug]/Kd(drug) = [GTP]/Kd(GTP) = 50,000,000, giving Kd(drug) = (5×10⁻⁶ M)/(5×10⁷) = 1×10⁻¹³ M (0.1 pM). That sub-picomolar requirement explains why reversible competition fails and covalent or separate-site binding is needed.
cards.quote: That huge affinity gap—plus early structures showing no obvious groove—made Ras the standard "undruggable" target.
cards.section: The target nobody could hit: a bond to the mutation itself

cards.front: What two molecular obstacles originally made K-Ras the standard "undruggable" target?
cards.back: Its huge affinity gap against reversible competitors in abundant cellular GTP (~50,000,000 [L]/Kd ratio) and early crystal structures showing no obvious drug-binding groove.
cards.quote: That huge affinity gap—plus early structures showing no obvious groove—made Ras the standard "undruggable" target.
cards.section: The target nobody could hit: a bond to the mutation itself

cards.front: What chemical handle does the K-Ras G12C mutation create that normal K-Ras lacks?
cards.back: Normal K-Ras has glycine (no side chain) at position 12, whereas G12C puts a cysteine there, exposing a reactive sulphur-hydrogen (thiol) group.
cards.quote: Normal K-Ras has glycine (no side chain) at position 12; G12C puts a cysteine there, exposing a reactive sulphur-hydrogen group (thiol).
cards.section: The target nobody could hit: a bond to the mutation itself

cards.front: Kevan Shokat's laboratory passed 480 disulphide-bearing fragments over purified GDP-bound K-Ras G12C and weighed the protein by mass spectrometry. Two fragments modified most of G12C, while normal K-Ras—with three cysteines elsewhere—showed no detectable reaction. What did this control prove?
cards.back: The fragments reacted selectively with mutant cysteine 12 rather than nonspecifically with native cysteines, and crystallography then revealed a hidden pocket beneath the switch II loop.
cards.quote: Two fragments modified most of the mutant; normal K-Ras, with three cysteines elsewhere, showed no detectable reaction.
cards.section: The target nobody could hit: a bond to the mutation itself

cards.front: How does sotorasib shut down K-Ras G12C without ever competing head-to-head against cellular GTP?
cards.back: In the transient GDP-bound state, sotorasib binds beneath switch II, covalently bonds cysteine 12, tilts Ras toward GDP, and impairs Raf binding for the protein's life.
cards.quote: Bonded to cysteine 12, sotorasib tilts Ras toward GDP and impairs Raf binding for the protein's life, never fighting GTP.
cards.section: The target nobody could hit: a bond to the mutation itself

cards.front: A tumour carries K-Ras G12V (valine at position 12) or G12D (aspartate at position 12), and the switch II pocket can still open. Would sotorasib form its permanent bond, and why?
cards.back: No. Neither valine's plain hydrocarbon side chain nor aspartate carries a reactive thiol, so an open pocket alone gives sotorasib nothing to covalently bond to.
cards.quote: Its limit is its chemistry: G12D (aspartate) and G12V (valine) carry no thiol and require other strategies
cards.section: The target nobody could hit: a bond to the mutation itself

cards.front: Suppose a second mutation inside K-Ras G12C abolished its slow GTP hydrolysis while leaving cysteine 12 and the switch II pocket intact. Using the lesson's account of why sotorasib works, what would you expect for its effectiveness?
cards.back: By the lesson's account, sotorasib would be expected to work less well. It binds the GDP-bound shape that K-Ras G12C enters briefly because it still hydrolyses GTP slowly; without hydrolysis that route to the GDP-bound pool is removed.
cards.quote: Because K-Ras G12C still hydrolyses GTP slowly, it cycles briefly through its GDP-bound shape.
cards.section: The target nobody could hit: a bond to the mutation itself

cards.front: Why are therapeutic antibodies such as trastuzumab and cetuximab restricted to targets on a receptor's outer face?
cards.back: An antibody cannot cross the cell membrane, so it can only bind extracellular epitopes on a receptor's outer surface.
cards.quote: An antibody cannot cross the membrane, so it binds a receptor's outer face—trastuzumab (1998) and cetuximab (2004)
cards.section: Outside, inside, beside: five landing places, and what the network does next

cards.front: An {{c1::allosteric inhibitor}} binds next to an enzyme's active site and locks the enzyme off, as MEK inhibitors do in a pocket particular to MEK.
cards.quote: An allosteric inhibitor binds next to the active site and locks the enzyme off—MEK inhibitors (Ras and MAPK lesson) fit a pocket particular to MEK.
cards.section: Outside, inside, beside: five landing places, and what the network does next

cards.front: Targeted signalling drugs need not inhibit enzymes: {{c1::venetoclax}} acts by filling BCL-2's protein-docking groove.
cards.quote: A target need not be an enzyme: venetoclax (cell death lesson) fills BCL-2's protein-docking groove.
cards.section: Outside, inside, beside: five landing places, and what the network does next

cards.front: A MEK inhibitor blocks MEK in the MAPK pathway, lowering ERK activity. How does the upstream cascade respond, and why?
cards.back: Upstream steps push harder and can partly switch the pathway back on. Normally ERK sends negative feedback to upstream steps, so blocking MEK relieves that feedback.
cards.quote: Block MEK, and that feedback is relieved, so the upstream steps push harder and the pathway can partly switch itself back on.
cards.section: Outside, inside, beside: five landing places, and what the network does next

cards.front: A lung cancer initially shrinks on an EGF receptor inhibitor and later regrows with an unchanged EGF receptor and extra copies of the MET gene. Why did the tumour resume growing?
cards.back: Network bypass. Extra copies of MET reactivate the same downstream signalling pathways that the EGF receptor previously drove, bypassing the blocked EGF receptor.
cards.quote: A bypass is the other network answer: in some lung cancers treated with an EGF receptor inhibitor, extra copies of MET reactivate the same downstream pathways.
cards.section: Outside, inside, beside: five landing places, and what the network does next

cards.front: In a K-Ras G12C tumour treated with sotorasib, upstream receptor signals surge and reload K-Ras with GTP. What happens to sotorasib's ability to trap K-Ras G12C, and why?
cards.back: Sotorasib traps less K-Ras G12C. Reloading Ras with GTP shrinks the GDP-bound pool sotorasib requires, which is why covalent compounds targeting GTP-bound K-Ras G12C are now in trials.
cards.quote: upstream receptor signals that reload Ras with GTP shrink the GDP-bound pool sotorasib needs; newer covalent compounds targeting GTP-bound K-Ras G12C are now in trials.
cards.section: Outside, inside, beside: five landing places, and what the network does next

cards.front: Combining the ERK negative-feedback rule with sotorasib's GDP-state requirement, predict how suppressing MAPK/ERK signalling with sotorasib in a K-Ras G12C tumour can cause the network to push back against sotorasib itself.
cards.back: Blocking MAPK/ERK signalling can relieve upstream negative feedback, so upstream receptor signals push harder and can reload K-Ras with GTP. That shrinks the GDP-bound K-Ras G12C pool sotorasib needs.
cards.quote: upstream receptor signals that reload Ras with GTP shrink the GDP-bound pool sotorasib needs; newer covalent compounds targeting GTP-bound K-Ras G12C are now in trials.
cards.section: Outside, inside, beside: five landing places, and what the network does next

cards.front: A tumour is driven by an intracellular GTPase with picomolar GTP affinity and a mutant-only cysteine beside an inducible pocket. Which landing strategy—antibody, reversible nucleotide competitor, or covalent mutant-residue binder—is viable, and what rules decide it?
cards.back: A covalent mutant-residue binder. Rests on the landing-place and competition rules: antibodies cannot cross the cell membrane, reversible competitors lose to abundant cellular GTP, and covalently bonding the mutant-only cysteine bypasses competition while sparing wild-type protein.
cards.quote: new sites and covalent bonds bypass competition, yet networks push back.
cards.section: A decoy in the receptor: fit without the push

cards.front: Because unstimulated beta receptors retain low basal activity, propranolol lowers signalling below rest and acts more precisely as an {{c1::inverse agonist}}.
cards.quote: unstimulated beta receptors retain low basal activity, and propranolol acts as an inverse agonist, lowering signalling below rest.
cards.section: Inverse agonism at the beta receptor

cards.front: Why does imatinib control chronic myeloid leukaemia without curing it, even when BCR-ABL is fully inhibited?
cards.back: Quiescent leukaemia stem cells survive full BCR-ABL inhibition, unlike rapidly dividing leukaemia cells.
cards.why: A second clinical limit is that inhibiting normal ABL, PDGFR, or KIT can occasionally injure normal tissue, with heart-muscle ABL a studied, though debated, case.
cards.quote: quiescent leukaemia stem cells survive full BCR-ABL inhibition, so the drug controls CML without curing it.
cards.section: Limits of kinase selectivity in patients

cards.front: A chronic myeloid leukaemia patient on imatinib acquires the T315I gatekeeper mutation in BCR-ABL. Combining the two-layer selectivity rule and imatinib's clinical off-target limits, what happens to the drug's balance of benefit versus normal-tissue risk?
cards.back: The benefit is lost while the off-target risk can remain. T315I stops imatinib from inhibiting BCR-ABL, yet imatinib still inhibits non-fused ABL, PDGFR and KIT in normal tissues, which can occasionally injure them.
cards.quote: inhibiting non-fused ABL, PDGFR, or KIT can occasionally injure normal tissue (heart-muscle ABL is a studied, though debated, case)
cards.section: Limits of kinase selectivity in patients

cards.front: Why did farnesyltransferase inhibitors, intended to block Ras's membrane lipid anchor, fail in K-Ras clinical trials, at least in part?
cards.back: A related enzyme attached a geranylgeranyl lipid instead of farnesyl, restoring K-Ras delivery to the membrane.
cards.quote: They failed in K-Ras trials partly because a related enzyme attaches geranylgeranyl instead, restoring membrane delivery.
cards.section: Lipid-anchor bypass and newer Ras drugs

cards.front: Besides GTP-state G12C inhibitors, what two strategies are being pursued to target K-Ras mutants such as G12D that lack cysteine 12?
cards.back: Non-covalent switch II pocket binders and chemistry that bonds directly to aspartate 12.
cards.quote: Reaching mutants without cysteine 12 now relies on non-covalent switch II binders (such as K-Ras G12D inhibitors) and chemistry bonding directly to aspartate 12
cards.section: Lipid-anchor bypass and newer Ras drugs
